analysis.one_liner: Imposed escalating fees on ozone-depleting CFCs and halons to fund research on safer substitutes.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: it got one subcommittee hearing, then died in committee with fees on CFCs left unenacted.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged CFC and halon producers and importers a fee per pound, rising to $2.50, scaled by each chemical's ozone-depletion power. It was designed to recapture the extra profits companies stood to earn when production caps raised chemical prices, and to route up to $100 million a year into a trust fund for research on substitutes and CFC-free products. The bill never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The public, through protection of the ozone layer and reduced greenhouse warming, since the charge pushes producers and users away from ozone-depleting chemicals [S2][S3]. Firms developing substitutes and CFC-free products also gain, because 30 percent of the first $100 million in annual charge revenue funds substitute-chemical research by chemical producers and 70 percent funds research into alternative products such as refrigerators, air conditioners, foams, and electronics made without CFCs [S2][S3]. Exporters get refunds on chemicals sold abroad, keeping them competitive [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an ozone-protection charge on producers and importers of five major CFCs starting July 1, 1989, rising from $0.25 to $2.50 per pound by 1993, and on three halons at $1.50 per pound starting in 1992, with the charge multiplied by each chemical's ozone-depletion factor so the most damaging chemicals cost the most.

Captures the windfall that producers would otherwise keep: the bill's findings state that production caps under the Montreal Protocol will raise CFC and halon prices, and the charge is calculated from the added revenues firms earn from those restrictions, so the public rather than shareholders keeps the extra money.

Creates an Ozone Layer and Climate Protection Trust Fund, with the first $100 million of annual charge revenue funding research: 30 percent for substitute chemicals by producers, 70 percent for alternative products made without ozone-depleting chemicals, including testing safety and improving energy efficiency.
Avoids penalizing legitimate chemistry by exempting chemicals that are used up entirely in producing other chemicals, and lets exporters claim refunds for charges paid on chemicals sold abroad.

Directs the EPA to add any chemical known to deplete ozone to the covered list and to adjust dates and charge levels as science and substitute availability change, so the program can keep pace with the problem.

analysis.who_pays: CFC and halon producers and importers pay the charge directly, up to $2.50 per pound, and would pass much of it on in higher prices to manufacturers of refrigerators, car and commercial air conditioners, electronic components, and foams, and ultimately to consumers of those products [S2][S3]. Producers also bear the cost of reporting revenues and cost data to the EPA for the charge calculation [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: CFC producers, importers, and downstream users

drawbacks.text: Higher chemical prices would flow through to everyday purchases: refrigerators, car and commercial air conditioners, electronics, and foam products would cost more during the transition away from CFCs and halons.

Only the first $100 million of charge revenue each year goes to the research trust fund; everything above that goes to the Treasury as general receipts, so most of the money collected would not be returned to the industry or the public in any earmarked form.

The charge calculation is complex: the EPA must estimate revenues, production costs, and a 'reasonable rate of return' from firm-by-firm reports, and companies can petition to adjust their cost baselines, inviting years of disputes over the number.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — protecting the ozone layer and limiting warming, with health effects like skin cancer risk — is large, and the design is smarter than a plain tax because it recaptures windfall profits created by production caps and recycles $100 million a year into substitute research. The costs are real but transitional and fall mostly on a small set of chemical producers, with modest price pass-through to consumers. The main honest criticism is administrative complexity and that revenue above $100 million a year simply joins general Treasury receipts.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and was never reported out, so it died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Max Baucus introduced the bill on March 2, 1989, with Republican John Chafee joining as the other original sponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
Four senators cosponsored the bill, three Democrats and one Republican.
The Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held hearings on May 19, 1989, but the full committee never marked up or reported the bill, and no Senate vote ever occurred.
The bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, leaving the charge and the research trust fund unenacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: CFC and halon producers and importers are better off, having avoided a per-pound charge that would have risen to $2.50 and a recapture of the extra revenue production caps would have created; the public did not get the dedicated ozone-research fund this bill offered.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill was bipartisan from the start, with a Democratic and a Republican original sponsor and cosponsors split 3 Democrats to 1 Republican.

industries.note: The bill taxes their output at rates rising to $2.50 per pound and specifically captures the windfall profits production caps would have created, with charges scaled by each chemical's ozone-depletion power. Only the first $100 million a year is recycled back to them, as research grants for substitute chemicals.

industries.industry: Refrigeration, air-conditioning, electronics, and foam manufacturers
industries.note: They would pay more for CFCs and halons as the charge raises chemical prices, but 70 percent of the research trust fund targets alternative products — CFC-free refrigerators, air conditioners, foams, and electronics — to help them compete in the worldwide shift away from these chemicals.

industries.industry: Importers and exporters of ozone-depleting chemicals
industries.note: Importers pay the same charge as domestic producers, removing any price advantage for foreign-made chemicals, while exporters can claim refunds for chemicals sold abroad, so the charge does not put them at a competitive disadvantage internationally.
